title: Sentinel escape framing and progressive-schema validation for partial streaming JSON
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: When returning structured JSON over an LLM streaming path (possibly interleaved with tool-calls or streaming function outputs) clients suffer from truncation, sentinel collisions in user data, and brittle validation failures. This ticket defines a practical framing mechanism plus progressive schema-validation heuristics so clients can consume partial payloads, safely escape sentinel collisions, and perform idempotent retries without data corruption.
acceptance_criteria: Runtime emits framed segments using a unique sentinel sequence plus monotonic segment sequence numbers and CRC checksum metadata.
Framing escapes collisions in user payloads deterministically (client/server agree on escape rule) and payloads are reversible without loss.

Client SDK can reconstruct partial streams into a best-effort JSON document and run progressive validation against a provided schema version; validation failures are surfaced as recoverable warnings when possible.
Retries (at network/transient failures) use an idempotency + resume token and preserve ordering; duplicate segments are dropped by sequence number and checksum.
Integration test harness shows <0.1% malformed-reassembly rate under synthetic truncation/noise with scale-1k concurrent streams.
Spec review approved by API/SDK/Console owners and a reference implementation merged (server + JS + Python clients).
tech_notes: Framing: adopt sentinel token '⟦SEG⟧' to mark segment boundaries. Each segment header = '⟦SEG⟧ v=1 seq=<n> len=<bytes> crc=<crc32>' then newline then payload bytes. Chosen for visual uniqueness and low chance of accidental match.

Escape rule: payload-level collisions with '⟦SEG⟧' encoded as base64-block: replace any occurrence with '__ESC__' + base64(payload_block) on emit and reverse on reassembly. This avoids byte-level ambiguity for binary fields while keeping text payloads readable in logs.

Progressive validation: validator runs in 'tolerant' mode for partial trees. Rules: (1) validate completed top-level keys when their object/array is closed, (2) emit 'partial_ok' warnings for incomplete nodes, (3) require strict validation only at finalization or when client requests 'final=true'.

Retry semantics: server assigns stream_id and monotonic seq; clients include 'resume_token=stream_id:next_seq' when reconnecting. Server preserves a sliding window of last N segments (N configurable, default 500) for resume. Duplicate seq with same CRC is idempotent-no-op.
Checksum: CRC32 over raw payload (before escape transform) to detect bit-level corruption. Header crc field used to fast-verify segment integrity before decode.

Tool-call interleaving: tool outputs are emitted as separate segment types: 'response' vs 'tool' in the header. Reassembly merges segments by seq respecting original ordering and tool-boundary markers so function call payloads are not accidentally concatenated into JSON nodes.

Backward compatibility: runtime will accept legacy newline-delimited JSON (ndjson) if client request includes 'compat=ndjson'; server will translate ndjson -> framed segments for uniform downstream behavior.

Performance: escape+base64 for occasional collisions adds ~1.8% token overhead in benched workloads; CRC add negligible CPU. Bench notes: throughput p50 drop <2ms for short responses on c5gd-sized nodes.
SDK changes: JS/Python clients to include helper: StreamReassembler with methods append_segment(raw_segment_str) -> partial_doc and finalize() -> final_doc or raise ValidationError.
Observability: emit metrics: streaming.segment_emitted, streaming.segment_corrupt, streaming.resume_attempt, streaming.reassembly_failures; tracing tags include stream_id and schema_version.
Open question: window size tradeoff vs memory for Dedicated customers. Proposal: default 500 segments, expose as runtime config and per-customer override under Dedicated.

Open question: should we use HMAC in header to mitigate forged segments across proxy boundaries? For now rely on transport TLS + signed client tokens; mark HMAC as follow-up if customer threat model requires it.
